name: chibi-scheme
desc: Small footprint Scheme for use as a C Extension Language
why: A tiny Scheme meant for embedding in C, a small and strange language world worth an afternoon of exploring.

brief.what_it_is: Chibi-Scheme is a very small Scheme implementation meant to be embedded in C programs as an extension and scripting language. It has no external dependencies and builds a shared library, libchibi-scheme, plus a sample chibi-scheme command-line REPL. Its default language includes the R7RS small bindings, a full numeric tower with rational and complex numbers, Unicode support, hygienic macros, and an extensible module system. Each VM runs in an isolated heap, so several VMs can run at once in different OS threads.
brief.why_it_exists: The README frames it as a small library for scripting inside C programs, saying it is "intended for use as an extension and scripting language in C programs." It aims to be easy to drop into any project while still doing "The Right Thing" by default despite its small size.
brief.how_it_works: The README describes VM-based lightweight threads and a separate heap for each VM, which lets multiple VMs run simultaneously in different OS threads. The language is built in layers, and the manual explains how to compile with fewer features or request a smaller language at startup. The README does not go deeper into the internals.

brief.install_notes: No external dependencies. Building uses make; the README notes that non-GNU make needs a few parameters in Makefile.detect set by hand. Installation defaults to /usr/local and can be changed with PREFIX. To run without installing, set LD_LIBRARY_PATH (DYLD_LIBRARY_PATH on macOS) so the shared libraries can be found. Native Windows desktop has basic support, with build instructions in README-win32.md.
brief.standout: It is designed to be embedded in C as a small library, and each VM gets its own isolated heap, so several can run in parallel OS threads. Despite the small size, the defaults include a full numeric tower, Unicode, hygienic macros, and R7RS small.
brief.status: unknown. The README shows no release date, version number, or last-commit date, and I did not check the commit history. It describes a broad list of supported platforms (Linux, BSDs, macOS, Plan 9, Windows, iOS, Android, ARM, Emscripten), but that does not show whether the project is currently active.
brief.caveats: Native Windows desktop support is described only as basic, and the README points to a separate file for it. The build relies on GNU make conditionals, and other makes need manual edits to Makefile.detect. The README does not state a license. The full documentation is in the manual, which I did not fetch.
